channel.title: Genomics Feed
channel.description: Aggregated research articles from Nature Genetics, Cell Genomics, Genome Biology, Genome Research, Nucleic Acids Research, and RNA.

item.title: Cell Genomics: NeoBridge: Biophysics-informed neoantigen prioritization and clonal architecture profiling in pancreatic cancer
item.description: Lana Mediavilla et al. present NeoBridge, a biophysics-informed machine learning ensemble that prioritizes immunogenic neoantigens. In pancreatic cancer, subclonal neoantigen load, not clonal load, associates with worse survival, suggesting that clonal architecture should inform vaccine target selection

item.title: Cell Genomics: Detecting low-allele-fraction mosaic mutations: A multi-institution benchmarking with cell-line mixtures
item.description: Ha et al. benchmark detection strategies for mosaic mutations with low variant allele fractions (VAFs) using short- and long-read whole-genome sequencing. By cross-validating Illumina-based calls against PacBio HiFi data using cell-line mixtures generated across five institutions, they construct stratified reference sets, define realistic detection limits, and establish best practices for genome-wide analysis of low-VAF (<2%) variants in non-cancer tissues.

item.title: Cell Genomics: A pangenomic method for establishing a synthetic somatic variant resource in HapMap mixtures
item.description: Kong et al. present a comprehensive resource for benchmarking somatic variant detection across variant classes and allele fractions. Using HapMap mixtures and pangenome graphs, they establish standardized benchmarking sets for evaluating sequencing technologies and variant-calling methods.

Nucleic Acids Research: The MODNAP benchmark set for modeling ribose-based modified nucleic acid and nucleic acid–protein complexes: a case study with AlphaFold 3
item.description: Abstract Modified nucleic acids play important roles in biology and biotechnology. However, their chemical and structural diversity as well as effects on nucleic acid structure and intermolecular interactions remain incompletely characterized. The performance of structure prediction and co-folding algorithms for modeling modified nucleic acids and nucleic acid–protein complexes has also not been evaluated. Here, we systematically analyze ribose-based modified nucleotides present in structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank. Modified nucleotides are primarily localized to the nucleobase, where they exhibit chemical and structural diversity shaped by molecular size, topological shape descriptors, and polarity-related properties. We develop MODNAP, the first curated dataset of experimentally determined structures containing modified nucleotides. Using MODNAP, we benchmark AlphaFold 3 on 1039 nucleic acid and nucleic acid–protein complex structures spanning a range of nucleotide modifications, tertiary folds, and biological functions. AlphaFold 3 achieves success rates exceeding 80% at an RMSD threshold of 2.5 Å. However, its accuracy in positioning modified nucleotides is variable and decreases for structures not explicitly represented in training. PoseBusters analysis reveals frequent intramolecular validity failures, primarily due to non-ideal ribose ring geometries. Together, these results establish MODNAP as a resource for evaluating and improving structure prediction methods for modified nucleic acids.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Chemically stabilized long antisense oligonucleotides perturb RNA exosome function
item.description: Abstract The interaction with intracellular proteins shapes the pharmacology and toxicity of RNA drugs like gapmers and siRNAs. Here, we identify the RNA exosome as a modification-sensitive interaction partner of long, chemically stabilized, single-stranded RNA drugs. Using proximity biotinylation proteomics, we observe preferential binding of the catalytic exosome subunits DIS3 and EXOSC10 to oligonucleotides stabilized by 2′-ribose modifications and phosphorothioate linkages. RNA drug binding correlates with exosome impairment as measured by dose-dependent stabilization of promoter upstream transcripts and accumulation of ribosomal RNA processing intermediates leading to reduced cell viability. Consistent with structural requirements for substrate threading through the exosome channel, oligonucleotides longer than 24 nucleotides can impair exosome function. Systematic variation of ribose and backbone chemistry reveals that exosome inhibition is highly sensitive to the spatial arrangement of chemical modifications and can be mitigated by incorporation of bulky 2′-MOE residues or alternative internucleoside linkages like mesyl phosphoramidate. In contrast to the clinically established RNA drug modalities, class-specific liabilities of emerging ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides remain poorly understood. Importantly, we demonstrate that ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides can be designed that preserve editing activity while minimizing exosome interference. These findings illuminate critical variables that must be considered in the safer design of next-generation RNA base editing therapeutics.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Choice of phenotype scale is critical in biobank-based G × E tests
item.description: Phenotype measurement scale has long been known to impact genetic inference, yet it is often ignored in modern studies. Costantino et al. characterize how the choice of phenotype scale affects the results of common analyses. They find that it can change GWAS hits and PGS × E interactions and influence PGS performance in specific subgroups.

item.title: Genome Biology: Poison exon splicing in the human brain provides a new paradigm for understanding and targeting neurological disorders
Nucleic Acids Research: Structural basis of assembly-dependent activation of the MAD3–MAD4 nuclease in the Pseudomonas aeruginosa MADS defense system
item.description: Abstract The methylation-associated defense system (MADS) is a bacterial antiphage immune system that cooperates with CRISPR–Cas systems to restrict phage infection. Within MADS, the MAD3–MAD4 module has been proposed to function as an ATPase–nuclease module related to the OLD nuclease family, but the molecular basis of its assembly and function remains unknown. Here, we combined cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, biochemical assays, and mutagenesis to elucidate the architecture and assembly mechanism of the MAD3–MAD4 complex. We found that MAD3 and MAD4 assemble into a stable 2:2 heterotetramer. Structural and biochemical analyses revealed that MAD3 alone lacks detectable ATPase activity, whereas MAD4 is insoluble when expressed alone. Assembly of the MAD3–MAD4 complex induces a conformational rearrangement in which MAD3 adopts an ATPase-competent dimeric conformation, while MAD4 is stabilized through intersubunit interactions. This heterotetrameric assembly exhibits both ATPase and DNA cleavage activities. Overall, our findings reveal the molecular basis of MAD3–MAD4 heterotetramer assembly and provide the first structural and biochemical insights into the function of the MAD3–MAD4 module within the MADS defense system.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: HURDLER: a cloning method to overcome length limits in designed repeat proteins
item.description: Abstract The number of internal repeat modules remains a major limiting factor in the construction and functional exploration of long repeat proteins. As a solution, we present High-Utility Recursive Directional Ligation for Extended Repeat proteins (HURDLER)—a modular cloning strategy combining codon optimization, seamless insertion of restriction sites, and modified recursive directional ligation. It presents a very robust technique to clone DNA for large repeat proteins, which may also contain non-repetitive parts, with high fidelity requiring a minimal number of individual cloning steps. Using HURDLER, we cloned designed armadillo repeat proteins with up to 85 internal modules, corresponding to >3700 residues. The method also generates intermediate variants with defined numbers of internal repeats, enabling systematic investigation of how the number of modules influences protein structure and function. HURDLER thereby provides a reliable solution to overcome restrictions in the overall number of internal modules used in the construction of very long repeat proteins. Such proteins are increasingly utilized as building blocks in macromolecular protein assemblies with defined structures.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Attribute Network-based Ranking (ANeR) identifies conserved translational fingerprints of M-phase
item.description: Abstract Entry into M-phase requires mRNA translation, but whether mitotic and meiotic divisions share a conserved translational programme and which newly synthesized proteins promote Cdk1 activation remain unclear. We developed Attribute Network-based Ranking (ANeR), a multi-objective network-based method that ranks mRNAs according to their proximity to a training group across heterogeneous two-condition omics datasets. Applied to 30 datasets covering mitotic and meiotic divisions, ANeR identified a conserved M-phase translational fingerprint. Benchmarking ANeR predictions against independent mitotic datasets, together with experimental validation in Xenopus oocytes, confirmed that ANeR prioritizes proteins whose accumulation increases during both mitotic and meiotic M-phases. Application of ANeR to the meiotic translational programme identified Fam76b and Cdca3 as previously unrecognized translationally activated regulators required for timely Cdk1 activation, demonstrating that ANeR can uncover new regulators of meiotic M-phase. Analysis of the oocyte translational programme established how broadly CPE/PAS regulatory rules apply, identified transcripts that do not conform to these rules, and experimentally validated their translational activation. Together, these findings establish that vertebrate mitotic and meiotic transitions share a conserved programme of translationally regulated transcripts and demonstrate that ANeR can identify new regulators of cell division. Broadly, ANeR provides a flexible framework for investigating diverse biological questions using a collection of two-condition datasets.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: RiboBA: a bias-aware probabilistic framework for robust ORF identification across diverse ribosome profiling protocols
item.description: Abstract By mapping ribosome-protected fragments genome-wide, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) has uncovered extensive translation beyond conventional coding sequences, revealing non-canonical ORFs (ncORFs) with roles in diverse biological processes. However, robust ncORF identification remains challenging when Ribo-seq datasets exhibit attenuated periodicity. Protocol-induced biases during library construction is an important contributor to this loss, yet most ORF callers do not explicitly model these distortions. Here, we present RiboBA, a bias-aware probabilistic framework for robust ORF identification from Ribo-seq data. RiboBA combines a generative module that jointly infers protocol-induced biases and codon-level ribosome occupancy with a supervised module that identifies translated ORFs and initiation sites from the bias-adjusted profiles. In simulations with known P-site positions, RiboBA improved exact nucleotide- and codon-level P-site assignment relative to a conventional fixed-offset approach. Across simulations and diverse empirical Ribo-seq datasets, together with orthogonal immunopeptidomics evidence, RiboBA accurately recovers protocol-induced parameters and improves ncORF identification, with pronounced advantages for RNase I libraries with attenuated periodicity, and for MNase and nuclease P1 datasets, while maintaining competitive runtimes. In a Drosophila case study, RiboBA identified candidate ncORFs with coding potential, including recurrent upstream translation in ThrRS and Mettl2 , linking ncORF translation to threonine-related translational regulation.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: A tripartite RpoS-CRP-cAMP-Cra circuit orchestrates metabolic reprogramming during stress adaptation
item.description: Abstract The alternative sigma factor RpoS (σ S ) governs stress adaptation in many bacterial clades, yet how it coordinates stress responses with metabolic demands remains poorly understood. Thus, by integrating RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and physiological and molecular assays, we redefined the RpoS regulon in Escherichia coli , expanding it to 667 genes and demonstrating that metabolic genes unexpectedly predominate over stress-response targets. RpoS directly drives a massive metabolic reprogramming event: it activates glycolytic and sugar transport genes while simultaneously repressing the trichloroacetic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. This metabolic pivot is finely tuned by a novel RpoS-CRP-cAMP-Cra tripartite circuit to balance energy efficiency with survival during stationary phase. Furthermore, we provide a mechanistic framework for RpoS-mediated bidirectional regulation rooted in σ S -factor competition, where transcriptional efficiency in the absence of RpoS dictates the regulatory mode: highly efficient promoters are repressed by RpoS displacement, whereas weak promoters are activated. This study advances our understanding of transcriptional precision during bacterial adaptation and offers an architectural blueprint for synthetic metabolic engineering.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Substrate energetics in non-templated DNA synthesis by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase
item.description: Abstract DNA polymerases typically use deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) for DNA synthesis, yet the contribution of the γ-phosphate to catalysis remains unclear. Here, we examine the role of substrate energetics in enzyme-catalyzed polymerization using a fidelity-independent model polymerase, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT). Relative to dNTPs, we find that TdT utilizes the canonical deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) with reduced rates and catalytic efficiencies, but diminished substrate bias. This lower specificity indicates that the γ-phosphate contributes primarily to nucleotide discrimination, rather than phosphodiester bond formation. Furthermore, our work shows that dNDPs and dNTPs with the same nucleobase exhibit comparable activation energies for the rate-limiting step during DNA synthesis, supporting a model in which the γ-phosphate is not required for lowering the energetic barrier for TdT-catalyzed polymerization. These findings define a mechanistic framework for understanding non-templated DNA synthesis and its application in enzymatic DNA synthesis technologies.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Clonal heterogeneity in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and its impact on tumor progression
item.description: This study uses single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma tumors to investigate tumor heterogeneity and clonal evolution, providing a valuable resource for this aggressive cancer.

item.title: Genome Biology: Hi-C derived insulation strength predicts evolutionary conservation of topologically associating domains
Nucleic Acids Research: Distinct ways by which Srs2 helicase and Rrp1 translocase shape Rad51–DNA interactions in fission yeast
item.description: Abstract Precise regulation of homologous recombination is essential for genome stability. Multiple helicases and translocases prevent toxic, unscheduled association of the Rad51 recombinase with chromatin, and their levels are frequently dysregulated in cancer. It remains unclear how anti-recombinogenic enzymes act on distinct pools of Rad51. Using Schizosaccharomyces pombe , we show that the Srs2 helicase and Rrp1 translocase may target distinct Rad51 species through recombinase substrate specificity and activity control. Genetic analyses support a model in which Srs2 may preferentially regulate Rad52-dependent Rad51 nucleofilaments associated with single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), whereas Rrp1 may preferentially regulate a distinct Rad51 population associated with double-stranded DNA. Accordingly, Rrp1 can alleviate the toxicity caused by Rad51 overproduction, a function not shared by Srs2. Unexpectedly, both loss and overproduction of Srs2 promote Rad51 accumulation, suggesting that excessive helicase levels may generate ssDNA substrates that promote Rad51 nucleation. Both Srs2 and Rrp1 fail to remove strand-exchange-deficient Rad51 from DNA. Both enzymes restrict Rad51 occupancy at centromeric regions, whereas only Srs2 acts within ribosomal DNA (rDNA) repeats, revealing locus-specific regulation. Our findings support a model in which anti-recombinogenic enzymes differentially regulate Rad51 according to its DNA substrate, thereby contributing to a regulatory system that balances Rad51 functions during DNA repair across different genomic regions.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: CircACVR2A(2–4) regulates stem cell pluripotency by uncoupling CDK-activating kinase functions
item.description: Abstract Differentiation of stem cells is driven by tightly coordinated transcriptional programs, yet the contribution of circular RNAs (circRNAs) to lineage specification remains poorly defined. Here, we profiled circRNA and messenger RNA expression during differentiation of human embryonic stem cells into five germ layer–derived lineages. Targeted silencing of dynamically regulated circRNAs revealed that depletion of circACVR2A (2–4), but not its linear counterpart, induced rapid loss of pluripotency accompanied by neuroectoderm-biased differentiation, phenotypically and transcriptionally. Mechanistically, circACVR2A (2–4) interacts with cyclin H within the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK)-activating kinase (CAK) complex to modulate RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) phosphorylation independently of CDK activation, with lineage commitment consistent with destabilization of RNAPII pausing at poised neuroectodermal loci. In vivo, circACVR2A (2–4) silencing impaired neuronal migration in the embryonic mouse brain and attenuated glioblastoma progression in mouse orthotopic xenografts. Together, these findings identify a circRNA-mediated mechanism that uncouples CAK complex activity to modulate stem cell fate.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Fast, flexible gene cluster family delineation with IGUA
item.description: Abstract Prokaryotic genomes harbor a variety of functional elements encoded as contiguous multi-gene clusters. To identify homologous gene clusters, computational tools that account for multi-gene architectures are needed to group gene clusters into Gene Cluster Families (GCFs). However, existing GCF delineation methods do not scale well to large datasets and are often limited to certain subclasses of gene clusters. Here, we present IGUA (Iterative Gene clUster Analysis; https://github.com/zellerlab/IGUA ), a scalable, flexible GCF delineation method for genomic segments with multi-gene architectures. On a biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) clustering task, IGUA is 29× and 10× faster than the state-of-the-art (BiG-SCAPE v2 and BiG-SLiCE v2, respectively; 28 CPUs), without sacrificing accuracy. To highlight its scalability, we use IGUA to cluster >2.8 million BGCs from ≈1 million prokaryotic genomes in <18 h ( n = 2 829 071 BGCs to 56 960 GCFs). To showcase its utility beyond BGC clustering, we use IGUA to cluster five additional prokaryotic gene cluster types (secretion systems, prophages, genomic islands, phage-plasmids, and carbohydrate active enzyme [CAZyme] gene clusters). Overall, IGUA represents a versatile GCF delineation tool with unmatched computational efficiency and flexibility, enabling (meta)genomic mining applications at unprecedented scales.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: ZBP1 specifically binds pre-formed Z-RNA, limiting its potential pool of nucleic acid ligands compared to ADAR1
item.description: Abstract ZBP1 senses foreign nucleic acids in the unusual, left-handed Z-conformation via binding through its Zα1 and Zα2 domains and initiates cell death pathways that enable viral clearance. dsDNA and dsRNA can adopt Z-conformations; however, both typically require chemical modifications or protein binding to induce Z-form conversion and stabilization. ZBP1 has been previously shown to bind and convert B-DNA to the Z-conformation and was assumed to be able to convert A-RNA as well, despite the lack of experimental validation. Here, we use NMR and other biophysical and biochemical experiments to characterize the Z-DNA and Z-RNA binding properties of ZBP1’s Zα1 and Zα2 domains. While ZBP1’s Zα domains are able to convert and stabilize unmodified dsDNA in the Z-conformation, they are incapable of flipping unmodified (CpG) n repeat dsRNA. ZBP1’s Zα domains require dsRNAs with Z-promoting chemical modifications to be able to bind and stabilize the Z-conformation. These results contrast with ADAR1’s Zα domain, which can bind and flip both dsDNA and dsRNA into the Z-conformation, potentially indicating finely tuned competition between ADAR1 and ZBP1 for pro-survival and pro-death outcomes, respectively. This work highlights the functional variability of Zα domains and narrows down potential physiological substrates of ZBP1 in infection and disease.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: PXL: a nucleic acid-binding module of the promyelocytic leukemia protein
item.description: Abstract The promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML) is a stress-response factor that assembles into PML nuclear bodies, dynamic subnuclear compartments involved in tumor suppression and antiviral defense. The most abundant isoform, PML-1, has been linked to transcriptional regulation, genome stability, and antiviral responses, yet the molecular basis of these functions remains unclear and is generally attributed to proteins associated with PML nuclear bodies. Here, we report that PML-1 itself harbors a previously structurally uncharacterized nucleic acid-binding domain. The domain, termed PXL, is encoded by exon 9 of the PML gene and is unique to isoform 1. Its structure reveals an exonuclease III fold, but lacks the catalytic residues required for activity, defining PXL as a pseudo-exonuclease. Biochemical, structural, mutational, and cellular analyses demonstrate that PXL specifically binds G-rich oligonucleotides implicated in G-quadruplex formation and displays a strong in vitro preference for polyUG RNA. Furthermore, deletion of the PXL domain significantly decreases PML colocalization with G-quadruplexes in cells, downregulates genomic maintenance pathways, and modulates the expression of E2F target and interferon-α response genes. These findings provide a molecular basis for previous observations implicating PML in nucleic acid-associated functions and establish a mechanistic framework for future studies of PML-mediated stress responses, nuclear organization, and gene regulation.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Double-base deletions and signatures associated with platinum adducts in metastatic cancer
item.description: Abstract Platinum compounds preferably create intrastrand G-G adducts to halt replication in cancer cells. When successfully bypassed, resulting somatic variants end up in the genome. Unexpectedly, current double-base substitution signatures associated with platinum lack a GG component, and we hypothesized that deletion was missing from the possible solutions to circumvent a double-base lesion. We investigated a large pan-cancer metastatic cohort and generated platinum specific de novo double-base substitution and deletion (DBSD) signatures. One of the oxaliplatin associated DBSD signatures had GG deletion as dominant characteristic and also included new and known substitutions associated with platinum. Unforeseen among the additional results, DBSD signatures with deletion of TT as singular characteristic were strongly associated with microsatellite instability in multiple cohorts and provisionally in liquid biopsies. This study showed that DBSD signatures increase our understanding and cataloging of the effects caused by platinum and, in general, may aid in the discovery of new biological insights.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Genomic sequence context differentially impacts stepwise oxidation by TET enzymes to shape DNA hydroxymethylation landscapes
item.description: Abstract Ten-eleven translocation (TET) enzymes reverse gene silencing imposed by 5-methylcytosine (5mC) in mammalian genomes by catalyzing the stepwise oxidation of 5mC to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), 5-formylcytosine (5fC), and 5-carboxycytosine (5caC). 5hmC both acts as an independent epigenetic mark and promotes replication-dependent DNA demethylation by antagonizing maintenance DNA methylation. Oxidation of 5hmC to 5fC/5caC instead marks the committed step in replication-independent DNA demethylation, whereby 5fC/5caC are actively excised and reverted to unmodified cytosine. Although prior work indicates that TET-mediated oxidation is influenced by bases neighboring 5mC, these studies have been unable to resolve more than two of the relevant species—5mC, 5hmC, and 5fC/5caC—at the same time. As 5hmC is the key fulcrum in DNA demethylation, we established a high-throughput enzymology approach to probe these three cytosine states at base resolution simultaneously across hundreds of sites. We reveal distinct context dependencies for 5hmC generation versus decay, with flanking bases differentially impacting 5hmC persistence. Notably, we demonstrate these predictable preferences in duplexed DNA are lost in single-stranded DNA, mechanistically linking these features to TET-mediated base-flipping. Furthermore, analysis of genomic 5hmC patterns uncovers evidence of sequence context bias in cellular 5hmC accumulation, suggesting a role for TET-intrinsic preferences in shaping cellular epigenetic landscapes.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: CRISPR-mediated gap-based replacement enables site-specific DNA lesion insertion into long DNA and nucleosomes
item.description: Abstract Defined DNA lesions are essential substrates for dissecting DNA repair mechanisms, yet existing approaches remain limited in positional flexibility, lesion diversity, efficiency, or compatibility with long and chromatinized DNA. Here, we present CGRID (CRISPR-mediated Gap-based Replacement for Insertion of DNA damage), a programmable strategy for site-specific installation of DNA lesions into long DNA and nucleosomes. CGRID uses paired Cas9 nickases to generate two adjacent nicks, followed by gap formation and replacement with a synthetic lesion-containing oligonucleotide. This design enables easy and efficient insertion of diverse DNA lesions at user-defined positions without pre-engineered nicking sites or substrate redesign. Applied to long λ-DNA, CGRID supports efficient installation of single lesions and internal double-strand breaks at predefined positions, which are challenging to obtain using existing methods. These molecules enable high-throughput single-molecule analysis of diverse repair pathways including base excision repair (BER), nonhomologous end joining, and microhomology-mediated end joining without hydrodynamic force. CGRID further allows efficient site-specific lesion incorporation into nucleosomal DNA, enabling systematic repositioning of damage within a nucleosome. This shows that nucleosome context and lesion orientation strongly influence APE1 incision efficiency. Together, CGRID establishes a broadly applicable platform for programmable DNA damage engineering, bridging biochemical and single-molecule methodologies, and facilitates mechanistic studies of chromatin-dependent genome maintenance.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Micronuclear ecDNA constrains tumor cell fitness and is associated with favorable patient survival
item.description: Single-micronucleus sequencing and live-cell imaging of cancer cells, as well as analyses of biopsies from patients with neuroblastoma, reveal that ecDNA in micronuclei limits tumor cell fitness and is associated with patient survival.

item.title: Genome Biology: Surface proteomics reveals arginine metabolism as a vulnerability in high grade serous ovarian cancer
Genome Biology: Integrating physiological and proteomics signatures for understanding drought, salinity and alkalinity stress tolerance mechanisms in lentil
Genome Biology: Identification of regulators of aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling in human cells by genome-scale CRISPR screening
Nature Genetics: Imputation of fluid intelligence scores reduces ascertainment bias and increases power for analyses of common and rare variants
item.description: Imputing unmeasured fluid intelligence scores in UK Biobank reduces ascertainment bias and increases power for genetic analyses, improving out-of-sample polygenic score performance and identifying rare variant signals that are strongly enriched for intellectual disability-associated genes.

item.title: Nature Genetics: A heritability-optimized method for functional prioritization of rare coding variants in complex traits
item.description: This study presents RovHer, a heritability-optimized scoring method for estimating the functional impact of rare variants, which is applied to the UK Biobank to demonstrate its ability to enrich for missense rare variants that maximally explain complex trait heritability.

item.title: Genome Biology: A curated genome-scale nucleotide diversity panel of non-human primates
Nature Genetics: Single-allele nanoscale mapping of regulatory variants
item.description: This study uses high-resolution, allele-specific chromatin architecture to identify causal gene-regulatory mechanisms in inflammatory diseases and uncovers a mechanism by which a neo-CTCF site promotes autoimmunity.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Reactivation of the embryonic ζ-globin gene ameliorates severe forms of α-thalassemia
item.description: Liu et al. identify cis -regulatory elements that silence the embryonic ζ-globin gene in definitive erythroid cells. Gene-editing strategies reactivate ζ-globin expression to therapeutically relevant levels in mouse and human disease models.

item.title: Genome Biology: Landscape and mutational dynamics of G-quadruplexes across the complete human genome
Genome Biology: Autumn–winter progression triggers distinct transcriptional programs in Arabidopsis thaliana
Nature Genetics: Single-cell profiling and genetic regulation of alternative polyadenylation in the human brain
item.description: This study provides a single-cell atlas of 3′ untranslated region regulation in the human brain, pointing to molecular mechanisms for genetic variants contributing to Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease and other brain disorders beyond gene expression.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Lineage identity governs oncogene dependence in mouse NSCLC models of KRAS inhibitor resistance
item.description: KRAS-mutant lung cancers frequently develop resistance to targeted inhibition. This study demonstrates that lineage plasticity shapes oncogene dependence during response and resistance to KRAS inhibition, establishing new models of histologic transformation.

item.title: Nature Genetics: CCNB1IP1 regulatory evolution underlies gradual increases in cortical size and folding in primates
item.description: The authors use tree shrews in multispecies comparisons to identify evolutionary changes in CCNB1IP1 expression associated with primate cortical expansion and folding, and investigate the cis -regulatory and molecular mechanisms through which CCNB1IP1 may influence these processes.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Disease-associated loci share properties with response eQTLs under common environmental exposures
item.description: Lin and Li et al. expose differentiating human stem cell cultures to nicotine, caffeine, or ethanol and identify genetic variants whose effects on gene expression emerge only after exposure. These context-specific regulatory variants resemble disease-associated loci, illustrating how environment-sensitive gene regulation can help explain signals from human genetic studies.

item.title: Nature Genetics: A human single-cell atlas identifies OLR1 + scar-associated macrophages as a potential therapeutic target for chronic liver disease
item.description: This study provides a single-cell RNA-sequencing atlas of 77 healthy and chronic liver disease livers and identifies a subpopulation of pro-inflammatory scar-associated macrophages enriched for OLR1 expression with therapeutic potential.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Germline homologous recombination deficiency influences TP53 -mutant clonal hematopoiesis fitness during platinum and PARP inhibitor treatment
item.description: The authors show that platinum is a greater driver of DNA damage response gene-mutant clonal hematopoiesis than poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors and that the presence of germline mutations conferring homologous recombination deficiency reduces the rate of expansion of these clones.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Single-cell multiomics across nine mammals reveals cell-type-specific regulatory conservation in the brain
item.description: Anderson et al. compare brain gene regulation across nine mammals, revealing that enhancer conservation extends beyond DNA sequence to include cell-type specificity and gene targets. Functional assays show how both ancient and human-specific regulatory elements shape brain biology and susceptibility to neurologic disease.

item.title: Genome Biology: Spatial and single-nucleus transcriptomics reveal the complexity of genomic imprinting in maize
Nature Genetics: Single-cell analysis of chromatin accessibility in the human intestine identifies regulatory programs and clarifies genetic associations in Crohn’s disease
item.description: This study uses single-cell ATAC–seq to map chromatin accessibility in the intestinal mucosa from patients with Crohn’s disease and healthy controls to characterize regulatory programs associated with inflammation and genetic effects.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Genome-wide mapping of common and rare variant effects on adiposity across childhood
item.description: Genome-wide analyses identify common and rare variants associated with childhood adiposity, including rare protein-coding variants in ADCY3 , CALCR , MC4R , MRAP2 , POMC and MYH13 that exhibit stronger effects in children than in adults.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Euchromatin forms condensed domains with short active regions on the surface
item.description: Simulations integrating micro-C and imaging data provide a coherent view of chromatin organization from nucleosomes to clutches to domains, revealing that most regions form compact domains but short regulatory elements are highly exposed.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Atlas of cell types and regulatory elements underlying human facial diversity
item.description: Single-cell transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility maps of the human craniofacial region in developing embryos provide insights into the mechanisms underlying facial variation and pathology.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Divergent medulloblastoma chromatin states disclose KDM2B as a selective dependency
item.description: Epigenomic analyses of medulloblastoma identify a bivalent/poised enhancer (EnhBiv) chromatin signature enriched for KDM2B binding in Group 3 and Group 4 tumors. Functional work suggests a selective dependency of these subtypes on KDM2B.

item.title: Genome Biology: The trajectory of KoRV-A evolution suggests initial integration into the koala germline genome near Coffs Harbour in New South Wales
Nature Genetics: Genetic factor analysis for characterizing phenome-wide patterns of genetic pleiotropy
item.description: Genetic factor analysis uses genome-wide association summary statistics to identify shared polygenic factors underlying patterns of cross-trait genetic associations, while automatically determining the number of factors and accounting for sample overlap.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Gb3 encodes a unique kinase fusion protein conferring greenbug resistance in wheat
item.description: Gb3 encodes an intracellular kinase–pseudokinase protein with a unique MAP3K-like domain that confers resistance to multiple greenbug biotypes in wheat.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Single-nucleus atlas of cell-type specific genetic regulation in the human brain
item.description: Multi-resolution genetic regulatory atlas of the human brain from single-nucleus transcriptomics of 1,384 donors of diverse ancestries reveals cell type-specific regulation underlying genetic risk of neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases.

item.title: Genome Biology: The Onychomys pangenome reveals the unique molecular adaptations that confer toxin resistance
Genome Research: Multilevel ensemble for genome-wide prediction of cell-specific G-quadruplexes utilizing transformed sequences and enhanced chromatin accessibility with G4Beacon2
Nature Genetics: Genetic landscape of an in vivo protein interactome
item.description: This study uses budding yeast as a model system to link genetic variants with quantitative changes in protein–protein interaction strength under different environmental perturbations by leveraging a protein-fragment complementation assay targeting 61 pairs of interacting proteins.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Concentrating cell-type-specific transcriptional signatures in bone marrow from interspecies comparisons
item.description: The authors present a framework to isolate condensed marker gene signatures by requiring both conserved cell-type specificity and conserved expression across multi-species scRNA-seq datasets. Bone marrow niche and hematopoietic progenitor signatures from four mouse species robustly resolve cell identity in two outgroup primate species, capturing highly conserved, biologically meaningful information.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Pre-diagnosis plasma cell-free DNA reveals early signatures of prostate and breast cancer risk up to eight years prior to clinical detection
item.description: Cheng et al. profile genome-wide cfDNA methylation in archived, prospectively collected plasma sampled 2 weeks to 9 years before breast or prostate cancer diagnosis. Regulatory-element signatures stratify future prostate cancer risk and reveal modest, heterogeneous breast cancer signals that vary by subtype, mammography interval, and progression to metastatic disease.

Cell Genomics: Mutation timing, accumulation, and selection in the male germline shape inheritance risk for developmental disorders
item.description: Neville et al. combine trio whole-genome sequencing with ultra-accurate sperm sequencing to quantify how de novo mutation timing and selection shape transmittable disease risk. Early embryonic mosaicism can create an uncommon elevated transmission risk, whereas universal age-associated mutation accumulation and spermatogonial selection account for most paternal pathogenic de novo mutations.

Cell Genomics: Single-library chromosome-scale diploid assemblies of vole genomes resolve a species-specific duplication implicated in pair bonding
item.description: Abuelanin et al. combine PacBio HiFi with low-coverage CiFi proximity-ligation reads in a single library and sequencing run to generate contiguous, near-telomere-to-telomere, accurately phased diploid genomes of prairie and meadow voles. These assemblies reveal strikingly rapid genome evolution, including near-complete Y chromosome divergence and a prairie-vole-specific Avpr1a duplication implicated in pair bonding.
